steps.b:
Atoms bond to reach a stable, noble-gas configuration (an octet). They do it in three main ways: by giving and taking electrons, by sharing them, or by pooling them.

Ionic: one person hands a coin to another and they stick like magnets. Covalent: two people share one umbrella. Metallic: a whole crowd under one big blanket of electrons.

An ionic bond (jonska veza) forms between a metal and a nonmetal. The metal gives electrons, the nonmetal takes them, and the opposite ions attract.

Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ and Cl (2,8,7) → Cl⁻, giving NaCl. Ionic compounds form crystal lattices, have high melting points, and conduct electricity when melted or dissolved in water.

Geology link: halite (NaCl) and fluorite (CaF₂) are ionic minerals; their cube-shaped crystals reflect the lattice.

A covalent bond (kovalentna veza) forms between nonmetals that share electron pairs: one pair in H₂ or Cl₂, two in O₂ (O=O), three in N₂ (N≡N).

  • Nonpolar: the same atoms share equally (H₂, Cl₂).
  • Polar: different atoms, the more electronegative one pulls harder and gets a partial negative charge (HCl, H₂O).

In a metallic bond (metalna veza), metal cations sit in a “sea” of free electrons — that’s why metals conduct electricity and can be hammered into shape.

steps.q: What kind of bond is in MgO, and how does it form?
s: Mg is a metal (group 2), O a nonmetal (group 16) → ionic.
O takes 2 electrons: O → O²⁻. The ions attract.

steps.e: Two identical atoms share a pair equally.
Metal K + nonmetal Cl → electron transfer.

steps.q: Which conducts electricity as a solid?
steps.e: Metals have free electrons. Solid NaCl doesn’t conduct — its ions can’t move.

steps.q: How many shared electron pairs are in O₂?
Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved in water.
steps.e: Dissolved ions are free to move and carry charge.
